skeleton:
Kebda Iskandarani

Egyptian · Medium · Serves 3–4

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
Alexandria's late-night carts sell kebda iskandarani — Alexandrian liver — to the crowds leaving the corniche: calf's liver diced small, fried fierce and fast with a mountain of green chilies and garlic, drenched in lemon, and scooped into bread with tahini and pickles. The dish is a ten-second stir-fry in a Mediterranean key: the heat does one thing, the lemon does another, and the liver must never learn what a slow flame feels like.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

Ingredients

- **Trim the liver ruthlessly and keep it cold.** Every trace of the ducts and membranes must go — they are the tough, bitter parts — and the dice goes back into the refrigerator until the pan is ready. Cold dice into a hot pan is the tenderness law; warm liver into a warming pan is the opposite. - **The bridge:** calf's liver is the Alexandrian cut; beef liver bridges, and chicken livers run a softer cousin (half the frying time). The tahini and pickles are the #9 ta'ameya cart's own shelf.

Kebda Iskandarani

Prep: 25 minutes · Cook: 10 minutes · Total: About 40 minutes · Serves 3–4

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 600 g fresh calf's or beef liver, trimmed of connective tissue, cut to a 1 cm dice (about 550 g trimmed)
  • 6 cloves garlic (about 25 g), sliced thin; 4 green chilies, sliced in rings (or 2, timidly)
  • 1 tsp cumin; ½ tsp coriander; ½ tsp chile flakes; salt and pepper
  • 3 tbsp neutral oil (about 40 g); the juice of a large lemon (about 45 ml), plus wedges at the table
  • A handful parsley (about 10 g), chopped
  • To serve: 4 rounds of bread (about 250 g), tahini sauce (4 tbsp tahini, about 60 g, thinned with lemon and water), pickled cucumber and turnip, and more chili

Instructions

  1. **Sear fierce, in two batches (90 seconds a batch).** Heat the oil in the widest pan you own over the highest flame until it shimmers; add half the liver in a single uncrowded layer and do not touch it for 40 seconds — then toss once, add half the garlic and chilies, and fry 30 seconds more. The liver's edges should brown, its centers stay rosy. Out of the pan; the second batch the same. Checkpoint — the pan must roar: a liver dice that hears a sizzle cooks in ninety seconds to a rosy medium; one that hears a simmer turns gray and firm in the same time. Crowding is the enemy — two batches minimum, three if the pan runs small.
  2. **The return and the drench (30 seconds).** Return all the liver to the hot pan off the flame, season hard with the cumin, coriander, chile, salt, and pepper, and drench with the lemon juice — the pan's heat flashes the juice's steam, and the liver drinks it. Checkpoint — the finished kebda should be glossy, browned at its edges, and warm-rosy within — a blood-red center is under, a gray-brown one is over, and the rosy midpoint is the dish's whole window. Taste: garlic and chili in the ascendant, cumin's earth, the lemon's sharp flood.
  3. **Serve immediately in bread, the full stack.** Bread split, tahini's thin spread, the hot liver spooned in with its chilies, pickles and a chili ring tucked, parsley over, a final lemon squeeze. Checkpoint — eating test: the bread's give, the liver's creamy-firm bite — iron-rich, lemon-bright, chili-fired — the tahini's cool and the pickles' sour cutting between bites. It should be loud, fast, and alive, the corniche at midnight in a sandwich, and a second sandwich is the tradition.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Liver gray, firmPan under-hot or over-crowdedThe roar, the batches, 90 seconds
Liver bleeding raw at centerDice too largeA 1 cm dice, honestly
Gritty biteDucts and membrane untrimmedThe ruthless trim, always

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- Liver waits for no one: trimmed raw keeps 1 day refrigerated, cooked keeps 1 day and re-fries fiercely hot (a fair second life). The sandwiches are assembled in the minute. - Variations: the chicken-liver version (softer, half the clock), the extra-chili corniche register. The #9 ta'ameya cart is this dish's street-mate; the #19 kefta mkaouara is kebda's tagine cousin on this site.

methodSteps.chefsNote: kebda iskandarani is the Mediterranean's answer to the stir-fry, and its doctrine is the sister site's wok law verbatim: the hottest pan, the smallest dice, the shortest clock, batches not crowds. The lemon-drench off the flame is the one Alexandrian addition — acid as a finishing cooking medium, flashed to steam — and it is a move worth stealing for every fast-fried liver on earth. The dish's window from perfect to over is measured in seconds; the carts' fame was built on those seconds, consistently won.
